title: Links & Navigation 🧭
description: Craft meaningful links and navigation patterns that work for everyone.

slides.title: The Humble Anchor Tag 🔗
slides.content:
`<a>` creates a hyperlink – one of the web's most fundamental interactions.

* It must have an `href` to be focusable.
* Screen readers announce it as "link".
* The **accessible name** comes from the link text, not the URL.

**Good**: "Read our accessibility report"
**Bad**: "Click here"

quizData.question: Which link text is most accessible?
quizData.explanation: Descriptive text helps users understand where the link leads; screen reader users often skim links out of context.

slides.title: Navigation Patterns 🧩
slides.content:
Navigation should be wrapped in `<nav>` – this creates a landmark that can be skipped to or skipped over.

* Use unordered lists (`<ul>`) inside `<nav>` – this announces the structure.
* Clearly indicate the current page (e.g., `aria-current="page"` on the active link).
* Avoid image‑only links without text – always provide an accessible name.

quizData.question: Why use `aria-label` on `<nav>`?
quizData.explanation: When you have more than one `<nav>`, labels like 'Main' and 'Footer' help users identify each one.

slides.title: Buttons vs. Links ⚔️
slides.content:
This is a common mistake:

* **Link (`<a>`)** – navigates to another URL.
* **Button (`<button>`)** – performs an action on the current page.

Never use a link styled as a button for actions like "Delete" – it confuses assistive tech. Use `<button>`.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Test Your Links
Navigate your page using a screen reader's **links list** (VoiceOver Rotor → Links). If you see multiple 'Learn more' links, you have a problem.
